## Introduction

::: {.callout-tip}
### Definition
A [**class**]{.sage} in C++ is a user-defined type or data structure that has [*data*]{.terracotta} and [*functions*]{.terracotta} (referred to as *members*). 

Instances of a class data type are known as [**objects**]{.sage} and can contain member variables, constants, member functions, and overloaded operators defined by the programmer. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%2B%2B_classes)
:::

:::: {.columns .hcenter}
::: {.column width=40%}
::: {.fragment style="margin: auto;"}
```cpp
class Point {
public:
  double x;
  double y;
};

int main() {
  Point pt;
}
```
:::
:::
::: {.column width=40%}
::: {.fragment style="margin: auto;"}
```cpp
class FourMomentum {
public:
  double E;
  double px;
  double py;
  double pz;

  double mass() {return std::pow(E*E - px*px - py*px - pz*pz, 0.5)}
};
```
:::
:::
::::

## Real-life example

```cpp
#ifndef Ising_h
#define Ising_h

#include <string>
#include <cmath>
#include <random>
#include <iostream>
#include <fstream>
#include <vector>


class Ising {
public :

  typedef std::vector<std::vector<double> > matrix_dtype;
  typedef std::vector<std::vector<int> > matrix_itype;

  Ising(double iJ=1.0, int iL=10, int iN_flips_per_step = 100, double iT=2.0, double iH=0.0);

  void resetAverages();
  
  void computeBoltzmannFactors();

  void thermalize(unsigned int n_therm);

  bool metropolisStep();

  void oneMCStepPerSpin();

  double magnetizationPerSpin();

  double energyPerSpin();

  void run(int n_mc_steps);

  double get_mAvg() const { return mAv_;}
  double get_m2Avg() const { return m2Av_;}
  double get_eAvg() const { return eAv_;}
  double get_e2Avg() const { return e2Av_;}

  std::vector<double> const & get_m_vals() const { return m_vals_; }
  std::vector<double> const & get_E_vals() const { return E_vals_; }

protected : 
  // C++11 random number generator from Mersenne twister. 
  std::random_device rd_;
  std::mt19937 rng_;
  std::uniform_real_distribution<> uniform_;
  

  double J_;                       // ferromagnetic coupling
  int L_, Lx_, Ly_;                // number of spins in x and y
  int N_spins_;
  int N_flips_per_step_;           // number of flips per recorded Metropolis-Hastings step
  matrix_itype spins_;                 // the spins
  double T_;                       // temperature
  double H_;                       // magnetic field
  bool thermalized_; // Did we run the thermalization yet?

  double w_[17][3];                // Boltzmann factors

  double acceptance_ratio_;
  int steps_;                      // steps so far

  double mAv_;
  double m2Av_;
  double eAv_;
  double e2Av_;

  std::vector<double> m_vals_, E_vals_; 
};

#endif
```

## Accessing member data

- Accessing the data inside a class:

::: {layout-ncol=2}
```cpp
Point my_point;
my_point.x = 1.; // <1>
my_point.y = 3.;

Point * point_ptr = new Point();
point_ptr->x = 1.; // <2>
point_ptr->y = 3.;
```

1. For a variable of the class type itself, use `.` to access its members.
2. For a *pointer*, use `->` instead. 
:::

---

## Methods

- Methods are functions defined *within* a class.

```cpp
class Point {
public:
  double x;
  double y;
  void print() const {
    std::cout << "(" << x << ", " << y << ")" << std::endl;
  }
}
```

- Class member functions are only accessible via an object ("instance") of the class, also using `.`
  - (Or a pointer to the object: `->`)
- The function is not generally accessible otherwise. 

```cpp
my_point.print();
point_ptr->print();
print(); // Compiler error: print is not defined outside of class scope
```

---

## Creating and destroying

- C++ gives you control over the **creation** and **destruction** instances of your class.

::: {.callout-tip}
### Definition
The [**constructor**]{.terracotta} is a special member function for creating an object of your class type.

The [**destructor**]{.terracotta} is a similar function for destroying the object (e.g. cleaning up heap memory).
:::

::: {layout-ncol=2}
```cpp
class Point {
public:
  Point(double ix=0., double iy=0.) { // <1>
    x = ix;
    y = iy;
  }
  ~Point() {} // <2>
  double x;
  double y;
  void print() const {
    std::cout << "(" << x << "," << y << ")" << std::endl;
  };
};
```

1. Constructor: function name is the same as the class name: `Point();`
2. Destructor: function name is the class name with a tilde: `~Point();`
:::

---

## Data protections

- We have seen a few examples of C++ providing guardrails on variables:
  - Scope (global, local)
  - `const`
- C++ defines 3 levels of access to a class's members:
  - `public`: anything can access.
  - `private`: only the class itself can access
  - `protected`: like private, but derived classes can also access (more on this later).
- Principle of least privilege: *make everything private*, unless it really needs to be public. 
  - One mindset: the public members define the **interface**, while private members define the **implementation**. 
- `const` also exists for classes... which can get complicated!


---

## Data protection example

- Let's apply "least privilege" to the Point class:

::: {layout-ncol=2}
```cpp
class Point {
public: // <1>
  Point( double ix=0., double iy=0.) { x_=ix; y_=iy;} 
  ~Point() {}
  void print() const {
    std::cout << "(" << x_ << "," << y_ << ")" << std::endl;
  };
  double x() const { return x_;}
  double y() const { return y_;}

private: // <2>
  double x_;
  double y_;
};
```

1. Constructor, destructor, and print functions are all public; these are the *interface* that users of this class need to interact with it.
2. Data members are private: cannot be accessed directly, but only through the interface 
:::

:::: {.r-stack}
::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=0}
- [**Interface**]{.sage} philosophy: developer defines *exactly* how class is used
  - `x()`, `y()` are called *getter* functions. 
  - Similarly, you could write *setter* functions for modifying `x_` and `y_`. 
  - User cannot arbitrarily modify class members.
:::
::: {.fragment .fade-in fragment-index=1}
- What about `const`?
  - Consider creating a `const Point`: getter and setter functions can modify the `Point`! 
  - Solution: mark functions as `const` if they do not modify `Point`. This lets the compiler know that those functions are legal for a `const Point`. 
:::
::::

---

## Operators

- Besides traditional named functions (`ThreeVector::length()`), C++ also lets you define the behavior of almost any operator. 
- Example: suppose we want to define the operator `+` for `Point`.

---

## Operator definition

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=50%}
```cpp
#include <Point.h>

int main() {
  Point p1(1., 2.);
  Point p2(5., 7.);
  Point p3 = p1 + p2; // p3 = (6., 9.)

  Point p4 = (-1., 2.);
  p1 += p4; // p1 = (0., 4.)
}
```
:::
::: {.column width=50%}
::: {.fragment}
```cpp
class Point {
  ...
  Point operator+(Point const & right) const {
    Point retval( x_ + right.x_, y_ + right.y_ );
    return retval;
  }

  Point & operator+=(Point const & right)  {
    x_ += right.x_; y_ += right.y_ ;
    return *this;
  }
}
```
:::
:::
::::

---

## Example: defining +

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=50%}
```cpp
class Point {
  ...
  Point operator+(Point const & right) const {
    Point retval( x_ + right.x_, y_ + right.y_ );
    return retval;
  }
}
```

```cpp
Point p1(1., 2.);
Point p2(5., 7.);
Point p3 = p1 + p2; // p3 = (6., 9.)
```
:::

::: {.column width=50%}
:::: {.r-stack}
::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=0}
`p3 = ` [`p1 +`]{style="font-weight: 1000; text-decoration: underline;"} `p2`

- Call function `operator+()` on object `p1`

:::
::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=0}
`p3 = p1 +` [`p2`]{style="font-weight: 1000; text-decoration: underline;"}

- `p2` is the input argument to `operator+(Point const & right)`
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in fragment-index=1}
```cpp
Point operator+(Point const & right) const {
  Point retval( x_ + right.x_, y_ + right.y_ );
  return retval;
}
```

- `operator+()` returns a newly created `Point`. 
- `p1` is not modified, so `operator+()`, so we mark it as `const`.
  - Similarly, `p2` is not modified, so `Point & right` is `const`, too.
:::
::::

:::
::::

---

## Example: defining +=

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=50%}
```cpp
class Point {
  ...
  Point & operator+=(Point const & right)  {
    x_ += right.x_; y_ += right.y_ ;
    return *this;
  }
}
```

```cpp
Point p1(1., 2.);
Point p2(5., 7.);
p1 += p2;
```
:::

::: {.column width=50%}
:::: {.r-stack}
::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=0}
[`p1 += `]{style="font-weight: 1000; text-decoration: underline;"} `p2`

- Call function `operator+=()` on object `p1`

:::
::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=0}
`p1 += ` [`p2`]{style="font-weight: 1000; text-decoration: underline;"}

- `p2` is the input argument to `operator+=(Point const & right)`
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in fragment-index=1}
```cpp
  Point & operator+=(Point const & right)  {
    x_ += right.x_; y_ += right.y_ ;
    return *this;
  }
```

- `operator+=()` modifies `p1` itself
  - *Not `const`*! Members (`p1.x_` and `p1.y_`) are altered
- Returns a reference to itself (we just throw it away; but this trick is useful for *operator chaining*)
  - `this` is a keyword meaning "pointer to myself"
- `p2` is not modified, so we should still mark the input argument `right` as `const`.

:::
::::

:::
::::

## Checkpoint

- **Classes** let you define your own structures with data and functions.
  - Introduced basic syntax.
  - Concepts of public, private, const for classes and their members.
  - **Operator overloading** lets us define sensible `+`, `-`, `+=`, `-=` (etc... `*`, `/`, `++`, `<`, `==`, `<<`, `[]`, even `()`) for our class.

```cpp
Point sum = p1 + p2;
Point dif = p1 - p2;
sum += p1;
dif -= p2;
```

# Structuring a program

- Header files
- Makefiles

---

## Class declarations vs. definitions

- Just like with functions, classes can have separate declarations and definitions.
- Usually, you put these in separate files:

 | |
--- | --- | ----
Header | `Point.h` | Declarations
Source | `Point.cc` | Definitions

- This lets you separate the compilation of Point from everything else.
  - **Modularity** is essential for large projects, where recompiling the whole project can take hours or days.
- Exception: templated code all goes in the header.

---

## Header files

- Actually, every piece of code we've seen so far has included a header:

```cpp
#include <iostream>
```

- To use `Point` in your `int main()` function, we just add this at the top:

```cpp
#include "Point.h"
```

- This lets `int main()` know all the essential info of class `Point`, without needing to compile it directly.
- The compiler takes care of **linking** the actual machine code for `Point`.
- Note the `include "xyz.h" versus `include <xyz>:
  - `""`: Looks in current directory.
  - `<>`: Looks in "default" directories

---

## Caveat: duplicate declarations

- When including header files, it's easy to duplicate declarations!
- Example: what if you `#include<iostream>` in `Point.h` and the executable, `read_points.cc`?
  - If  compiler should complain about redefining the same variables!
- Solution: use a "trick" using [*preprocessor directives*]{.blue}:

```cpp
#ifndef Point_h
#define Point_h
class Point {
  <bla bla bla>
};
#endif
```

---

## Recap: header files

- tl;dr: your multi-file program will look something like this:
  - **Declare** a class in the header file
  - **Define** the class in the source file
  - **Compile** the source into an object library
  - **Link** the "main" source file to the object library
  - **Execute** the program

## Makefiles

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=40%}

- A [**Makefile**]{.terracotta} semi-automatically compiles multiple files, following a rules-based input.
- Example: `ReviewCpp/ClassExample/Makefile`

:::
::: {.column width=60%}

```makefile
make_a_point: Point.cc Point.h make_a_point.cc
	g++ -o make_a_point Point.cc make_a_point.cc -I.

read_points_example: Point.cc Point.h read_points_example.cc
	g++ -o read_points_example Point.cc read_points_example.cc -I.

all: make_a_point read_points_example

clean:
	rm -f *.o *~ make_a_point read_points_example
```

:::
::::

---

## Makefiles

```
make_a_point: Point.cc Point.h make_a_point.cc
	g++ -o make_a_point Point.cc make_a_point.cc -I.
```

- **Target** (`make_a_point`): just a name for the rule
- **Dependences** (`Point.cc Point.h make_a_point.cc`): what's needed for this target
- **Rule** (`g++ -o make_a_point...`): command to execute for this target

---

## Makefiles

- Our Makefile has two more rules: "all" compiles both targets, and "clean" deletes the executables.
  - Running "make all" will compile both programs
  - Running "make clean" will delete both programs

```makefile
all: make_a_point read_points_example
clean:
  rm -f *.o *~ make_a_point read_points_example
```

---

## Makefiles

- Makefiles can get really fancy! (Aka extremely complicated)
- You're encouraged to read about them, but are not really responsible for writing them (I'll provide them where needed).
- Example: in `CompPhys/ReviewCpp/BasicExample`, you can compile all the cc files in a directory

```makefile
CXX = g++
CXXFLAGS = -std=c++11
all: $(patsubst %.cc, %.out, $(wildcard *.cc))
%.out: %.cc Makefile
$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) $< -o $(@:.out=)
clean: $(patsubst %.cc, %.clean, $(wildcard *.cc))
%.clean:
rm -f $(@:.clean=)
```

::: aside
Copied from https://stackoverflow.com/questions/9787160/makefile-that-compiles-all-cpp-files-in-a-directory-into-separate-executable
:::

---

## Checkpoint

- Structuring a program
  - Separate class declaration and definition into a header file and a source file.
  - `#include` the header files to use the class in your executable.
  - Makefile can help semi-automate the compilation.


:::{.mermaid-box style="width: 40%; min-width: 300px; height: auto; display: block; margin: 0 auto;"}
```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[BaseClass] --> B[DerivedClass1]

    classDef box fill:#e2745c,stroke:#e2745c,color:#ffffff,font-weight:bold,text-align:center;
```

:::: {.columns .hcenter}
::: {.column width=50%}
::: {.fragment}
- **Inheritance**: `DerivedClass` *is* a `BaseClass`. 
- `DerivedClass` "inherits" all the members (variables and methods) of `BaseClass`. 
- Then, you can add members to `DerivedClass`, or even *override* (redefine) methods.
:::
:::

::: {.column width=50%}
::: {.fragment}
- Why? 
  - You can write cleaner, more efficient, and better organized code. 
  - A good class hierarchy mirrors how humans think about "objects"
:::
:::
::::

---

## A concrete example

- Think about the difference between the relationships "has a" and "is a":
  - A Honda [*has a*]{.terracotta} motor.
  - A Honda [*is a*]{.blue} car.
- How would we write this as a data model in a program?
  - [*has a*]{.terracotta}: member variable of a class.
  - [*is a*]{.blue}: specific relationship between different classes, implemented with inheritance.

---

## Syntax

`cpp
class BaseClass {...}
class DerivedClass : public BaseClass {...}
``

- Syntax: just add `: public (ParentClass)` after the class name.
  - A detail: `public` here means the inherited parent variables will retain their access settings (public/protected).
  - Other options: `protected` or `private` if needed.

---

## A simpler example

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=40%}
- Simpler example: an HR record of a person working for NY state
  - A person has a first name
  - A person has a last name
  - A person has a NY state ID number
:::
::: {.column width=60%}
```cpp
class NYPerson {
public:
  NYPerson();
  ~NYPerson();
  std::string firstname();
  NYPerson& set_firstname(std::string ifirstname);
private:
  std::string firstname_;
  std::string lastname_;
  std::string ny_id_;
  };
```
:::
::::

## A simpler example

- What about a UB employee? They are a NY state employee, but additionally have UB info.
  - A UB employee is a NY state employee.
  - A UB employee has a UB ID number.

---

## A simpler example

:::: {.columns .vcenter}
::: {.column width=45%}
Base/parent class

```cpp
class NYPerson {
public:
  NYPerson();
  ~NYPerson();
  std::string ny_id();
  NYPerson& set_ny_id(std::string iny_id);
private:
  std::string firstname_;
  std::string lastname_;
  std::string ny_id_;
  };
```
:::
::: {.column width=10%}
[⟹]{style="font-size: 3em;"}
:::
::: {.column width=45%}
```cpp
class UBPerson : public NYPerson {
public:
  UBPerson();
  ~UBPerson();
  UBPerson& set_ub_id(std::string iub_id);
private:
  std::string ub_id_;
};
```
:::
::::

::: {.fragment}
- `UBPerson` inherits all the attributes (data, functions) from `NYPerson`: `firstname`, `lastname`, `ny_id`, `std::string ny_id()`, `set_ny_id()`
- `UBPerson` adds extra members for the UB ID
- Could even redefine methods if desired (e.g. return UB ID along with NY ID in `ny_id()`). 
:::

## class Car

- Back to the car example. Let's write some general code for cars, and specialize to specific cars.
- All cars use "energy" to drive. Let's give them some spatial coordinates and a drive function, plus "energy":

::: {style="width: 40%"}
```cpp
class Car {
public:
  void drive(double delta_t);
  void add_energy(double amount);
private:
  double energy_;
  double x_;
  double y_;
  double vx_;
  double vy_;
```
:::

---

## Gas vs. electric

- Next, specialize to gas vs. electric cars.
  - Both are cars, both drive following basic mechanics.
  - `add_energy()` is conceptually similar, but the implementation is very different!
  - Solution: **virtual functions**
    - Confusing word, but just means a function in `BaseClass` get [*overridden*]{.blue} in `DerivedClass`.
    - Use keyword `override` in DerivedClass for clarity (not strictly necessary).

:::: {.columns .vcenter}
::: {.column width=30%}
```cpp
class GasCar : public Car {
public:
  void add_energy(double amount) override {
    insertNozzle();
    fillGas(amount);
  }
}
```
:::
::: {.column width=5%}
[⟸]{style="font-size: 2em;"}
:::
::: {.column width=30%}
```cpp
class Car {
  ...
  virtual void add_energy(double amount);
```
:::
::: {.column width=5%}
[⟹]{style="font-size: 2em;"}
:::
::: {.column width=30%}
```cpp
class ElectricCar : public Car {
public:
  void add_energy(double amount) override {
    plugInCharger()
    recharge(amount);
  }
}
```
:::
::::

---


## Public, protected, private

- Aside: now we know enough to understand the 3 access settings for variables.
  - `public`: available to all code
  - `private`: available only within this class.
  - `protected`: available within this class, plus any [*derived classes*]{.sage}.
- Using the same keywords when declaring a derived class (`class GasCar : public Car{}`) lets you further control the access in the derived class
- And sub-sub-classes, etc.! 
  - E.g. `class Lambourghini : public GasCar{...}`

# Polymorphism

## Polymorphism

::: {.callout-tip}
### Definition
**Polymorphism** means writing code that works with objects of different types through a common interface, letting the actual type decide what happens when a method is called.

In practice, you call the same function name on different objects, and each one responds in its own way.
:::

:::: {.fragment}
- For our `Car` class, this lets us do something like:

```cpp
std::vector<Car*> cars;
Lambourghini car1; Rivian car2;
cars.push_back(&car1); cars.push_back(&car2);
for (Car * it_car : cars) {
  it_car->add_energy(100.);
}
```

::: {layout-ncol=2}
![](../assets/1.0_cpp/slide271_image46.png){width="70%" fig-alt="TODO: describe image"}

![](../assets/1.0_cpp/slide271_image47.png){width="70%" fig-alt="TODO: describe image"}
:::
::::


---

## Polymorphism

- In other words, we can call code from the *derived* class by accessing it through the *base* class. 
- This is handy: we can treat `car1` and `car2` in the same way (same code), and C++ figures out the actual implementation. 
- Another way of thinking: `car1` and `car2` share a  **common interface**; 

---

## Polymorphism: how it works

- Technical details: polymorphism uses something called a **virtual table** (vtable)
  - Each class stores a table of its functions (specifically, pointers to the functions in memory)
- At run time, your program figures out which virtual function to call: *dynamic/late binding*
  - Contrast with static/early binding: transformations performed at compile time
- To call derived class function, the program dereferences the pointer in the vtable
  - Depending on run-time value of objects, looks at a different class.
  - Sometimes degrades performance.

---

## Abstract classes

- Sometimes, you may want `BaseClass` to be **abstract**: not actually a real class that you want to use (e.g. pure interface with no implementations)
  - In our `Car` example, a generic "Car" doesn't really exist. 
  - So, we prevent the user from trying to instantiate the platonic ideal of "car"!
- Syntax: **set a virtual function to 0**:

```cpp
class Car { 
  ...
  virtual void add_energy(double amount) = 0;
}
```

- The virtual function is thus not defined, and the compiler will refuse to make a `Car`.

## Friendship

![](../assets/1.0_cpp/slide274_image48.png){width="70%" fig-alt="My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic movie poster"}

---

## C++ friend classes

::: {.callout-tip}
### Definition
**Friendship** is a relationship between classes that allow them to read private data.
:::

- Sometimes, you really need to access the private member data of another class. 
- Solution: friendship! Yes, friendship.
- This may not arise often in this class, but one common case is `operator<<` and `operator>>`. 

---

## C++ friend classes

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=50%}
- Friendship syntax: pretty simple. Remember the Mines of Moria?
  - "Speak friend and enter"

![](../assets/1.0_cpp/slide276_image27.png){fig-alt="TODO"}
:::
::: {.column width=50%}
```cpp
class A{
public:
  friend class B;
};
```

- Read as: `class A` grants `class B` access to all of its `private` and `protected` data members. 
:::
::::

---

## Example

- Common use case for friendship (a bit mercenary, no?): overloading the "<<" and ">>" operators:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=50%}
Header:

```cpp
class UBPerson {
public:
  ...
  friend std::ostream & operator<<( std::ostream & out, UBPerson const & );
  friend std::istream & operator>>( std::istream & in , UBPerson const &);
}
```
:::

::: {.column width=50%}
Source: 

```cpp
std::ostream & operator<<(std::ostream &out, StudentRecord const &right ) {
  right.print(out); 
  return out;
}
std::istream & operator>>(std::istream &in, StudentRecord  &right ) {
  right.input(in);
  return in;
}
```
:::
::::

# Class templates

---

## Templating and classes

- Templating works for classes just like functions.
- We've actually been using class templates a lot:
  - `std::vector<int>`, `std::vector<Car*>`.
- Now let's look a bit deeper

---

## Templating and classes

::: {style="margin: auto; display: block;"}
![](../assets/1.0_cpp/slide280_image24.png){fig-alt="TODO"}
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=50%}
- Remember back to function templates: they work like a cookie cutter
  - A cookie cutter is a template that you use to generate cookies
  - Cookies can be different types (chocolate chip, sugar, peanut butter, bacon, ...)
  - Similarly, a function template generates functions; input/return types can be different. 
:::

::: {.column width=50%}
::: {.fragment}
- Class templates work almost exactly the same:

```cpp
template<class T>
class Storage {
public:
  Storage(T in) {
    content_ = in;
  }

private:
  T content_;
}

int main() {
  Storage<int> int_store(2); // implicit instantiation
}
```
:::
:::
::::

---

## Class template syntax

- Similar to function templates, declare with `template <class T>`
  - Remember, `T` is a *placeholder* in this syntax. 
  - The template is not actually compiled; rather, the compiler uses it to generate code, doing a search-and-replace of `T` with a real type.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=50%}

```cpp
template<class T>
T squared(T x) {
  return x * x;
}
```
:::
::: {.column width=50%}
```cpp
template<class T>
class Point {
  T x;
  T y;
}
```
:::
::::

---

## std::vector<>

- `std::vector<T>` is a template!
  - `T` could be a float, int, UBPerson, Car*, ... or anything you want.
  - The operations of `std::vector` are the same regardless of type.
- The standard library provides the template, `std::vector<T>`. 
- You create actual classes, like `std::vector<int>` or `std::vector<UBPerson>`. 


---

## A warning

- If you do not correctly set up your templates, you will get sixty-seven pages of compiler warnings!
  - It issues the warnings for **every** instance of the class template. Consider if you defined 100 kinds of `std::vector<>`...
- Usually the first one is the one you care about, and it is actually usually descriptive, so READ THEM!

---

## Multiple template arguments

- You can even have multiple template parameters!
- Example: `std::map`, an associative container:
  - Equivalent to python dicts
  - Similar a vector, but lets you look up data by "key", which can by anything.
  - (You can also define a sorting algorithm)

```cpp
template<
  class Key,
  class T,
  class Compare = std::less<Key>,
  class Allocator = std::allocator<std::pair<const Key, T> >
> class map;

std::map<std::string, int> ppl_ages;
ppl_ages["John"] = 32;
ppl_ages["Bonnie"] = 56;

std::cout << "John age = " << ppl_ages["John"] << std::endl;
```

## 3-vector class template

- Two files:
  - `Vector3.h`: partially filled out class template for a 3-vector class. You should complete this file.
  - `make_a_vector.cc`: executable for testing your Vector3 class.
- Instructions (or just follow `Vector3.h` comments):
  - Create the member variables (`doubles x_, y_, z_`)
  - Create the "getter" and "setter" functions. Examples for the `x_` variable are provided, simply copy and modify for `y_` and z`_.
  - Create the `length()` function, which should compute `sqrt(x^2+y^2+z^2)`. (Use `pow(x, y)`)
  - `make vector3` to compile, `./make_a_vector.exe` to run.

---

## Bonus: sorting

- make_a_vector.cc also has an example of sorting a vector.

```cpp
// Sort the vector
std::sort(
  vlist.begin(),
  vlist.end(),
  [](const Vector3<double>& left, const Vector3<double>& right) {
    return left.length() < right.length();
  }
);
```

- `std::sort` takes 3 arguments: (1) iterator (think: pointer) to start of vector, (2) iterator to end of vector, and (3) a sorting function.
- For (3), we use a **lambda function**: a small, anonymous function created on the fly. See [https://www.w3schools.com/cpp/cpp_functions_lambda.asp](https://www.w3schools.com/cpp/cpp_functions_lambda.asp) for more details.

---

## Recap

- Inheritance lets us create general (/base/parent) classes, and then create specialized (/derived/child) classes that inherit and extend their functionality.
  - Example: class Car ⇒ class GasCar ⇒ class Lambourghini
- Polymorphism is a powerful C++ feature that allows us to transform objects between classes in our programs using inheritance.
- Friendship can be used to grant access to a class's private data.
- Class template work just like function templates, to define generic classes that work with arbitrary data types.
  - E.g. `std::vector<T>`, `std::map<K, T>`
